title: Bills that must originate exclusively in the House
ask: Under Art. VI, Sec. 24, which six kinds of bills must originate exclusively in the House of Representatives, and what may the Senate do with them?
items: Appropriation bills
Revenue bills
Tariff bills
Bills authorizing increase of the public debt
Bills of local application
Private bills
The Senate may ‘propose or concur with amendments’
src: Art. VI, Sec. 24; Tolentino v. Sec. of Finance
hook: ‘ART-DLP’: Appropriation, Revenue, Tariff, Debt, Local, Private.

title: The seven rules of Art. VI, Sec. 25
ask: State the rule in each of the seven paragraphs of Art. VI, Sec. 25.
items: (1) Congress may not increase the President’s recommended appropriations for government operations; budget form, content and preparation set by law
(2) No GAA provision unless it relates specifically to some particular appropriation; limited in operation to that appropriation (no riders)
(3) Congress’s own appropriations strictly follow the procedure for other departments and agencies
(4) Special appropriations bill must specify its purpose and be supported by available funds or a revenue proposal
(5) No law authorizing transfer of appropriations; five named officials may, by law, augment items from savings
(6) Discretionary funds for particular officials: public purposes only, supported by vouchers, subject to guidelines by law
(7) No GAA passed by the end of the fiscal year: the preceding year’s GAA is deemed re-enacted, automatically, until the new GAA passes
src: Art. VI, Sec. 25(1)–(7)

title: Requisites of a special appropriations bill
ask: What does Art. VI, Sec. 25(4) require of a special appropriations bill?
items: It must specify the purpose for which it is intended
It must be supported by funds actually available, as certified by the National Treasurer, or
by funds to be raised by a corresponding revenue proposal in the bill itself
src: Art. VI, Sec. 25(4)

title: Conditions on discretionary funds
ask: What four conditions does Art. VI, Sec. 25(6) attach to discretionary funds?
items: Appropriated for particular officials
Disbursed only for public purposes
Supported by appropriate vouchers
Subject to such guidelines as may be prescribed by law
src: Art. VI, Sec. 25(6); Belgica (2013) on presidential discretionary funds

title: The three rules of Art. VI, Sec. 29
ask: State the three rules of Art. VI, Sec. 29 on public money.
items: (1) No money paid out of the Treasury except in pursuance of an appropriation made by law
(2) No public money or property for any sect, church, denomination, sectarian institution, system of religion, or religious dignitary as such
(3) Taxes levied for a special purpose form a special fund, paid out for that purpose only
(3) If that purpose is fulfilled or abandoned, any balance goes to the general funds of the Government
src: Art. VI, Sec. 29(1)–(3)

title: Exceptions: paying a religious dignitary
ask: Under Art. VI, Sec. 29(2), public money may be paid to a priest, preacher, minister or dignitary only when assigned to which four institutions?
items: The armed forces
Any penal institution
A government orphanage
A leprosarium
src: Art. VI, Sec. 29(2)

title: General limitations on appropriations
ask: What are the three general limitations on the power to appropriate (class reviewer)?
items: Appropriations must be for a public purpose
No public funds or property for any religion or religious dignitary (Sec. 29(2)), save the listed exceptions
But a valid secular purpose that incidentally benefits a religion is allowed
src: Art. VI, Sec. 29(2); class reviewer (Part V.B.a)

title: Requisites of an appropriation ‘made by law’
ask: What makes something an appropriation ‘made by law’ under Art. VI, Sec. 29(1)?
items: It is made by law (a statute), not necessarily the GAA
It sets apart a determinate or determinable amount of public money
It allocates that money for a particular, stated purpose
That purpose must be public
Its primary aim is to appropriate; a bill creating an office and funding it is not an appropriation bill
src: Art. VI, Sec. 29(1); Guingona v. Carague; Belgica (2013); class reviewer

title: Kinds of appropriations
ask: What kinds of appropriations appear in the Constitution and the cases?
items: General appropriations (the annual GAA): Sec. 25(1), (2), (5), (7)
Special appropriations: purpose specified; funds certified available or a revenue proposal (Sec. 25(4))
Continuing or automatic appropriations, e.g., debt service, Malampaya Fund: no yearly re-enactment (Guingona; Belgica)
Re-enacted appropriations: last year’s GAA when no new GAA passes (Sec. 25(7))
Programmed versus unprogrammed: unprogrammed released only if revenues exceed targets (Araullo)
Line-item versus lump-sum appropriations (Belgica 2013; 2019)
Discretionary funds for particular officials (Sec. 25(6))
src: Art. VI, Sec. 25; Guingona v. Carague; Belgica (2013, 2019); Araullo

title: Four phases of the budget cycle
ask: What are the four phases of the budget cycle (Araullo), and who leads each?
items: Budget preparation: the Executive (President submits the budget within 30 days from the opening of each regular session, Art. VII, Sec. 22)
Budget legislation: Congress (cannot increase the President’s recommendations, Sec. 25(1))
Budget execution: the Executive alone (no legislator role: Belgica)
Accountability: audit by COA and congressional oversight (scrutiny and investigation)
src: Araullo; Belgica (2013); Art. VI, Sec. 25(1); Art. VII, Sec. 22

title: Budget rules outside Art. VI used in these cases
ask: Which budget rules outside Art. VI do the appropriation cases rely on?
items: Art. XIV, Sec. 5(5): education gets the highest budgetary priority, but Congress may still meet other needs (Guingona; Philconsa)
Art. IX-A, Sec. 5: Constitutional Commissions enjoy fiscal autonomy; approved appropriations automatically and regularly released (Macalintal 2023)
Art. VIII, Sec. 3: Judiciary’s fiscal autonomy; appropriations not reduced below the previous year’s; automatic, regular release
Art. XVIII, Sec. 3: prior decrees not inconsistent with the Constitution remain operative (debt decrees in Guingona)
src: Guingona v. Carague; Philconsa v. Enriquez; Macalintal v. COMELEC (2023)

title: Why automatic debt-service appropriations are valid
ask: Why did Guingona v. Carague uphold the automatic appropriation for debt service?
items: It is an appropriation ‘made by law’ (PDs 81, 1177, 1967); need not be in the GAA
Continuing appropriation: no yearly re-enactment needed
Standard 1: paid only as the loans fall due
Standard 2: the amount is determinable (only what is needed to service the debt)
The debt decrees survived 1987: not inconsistent with the Constitution (Art. XVIII, Sec. 3)
Education’s ‘highest budgetary priority’ does not hamstring Congress; education still got the highest department allocation
src: Guingona v. Carague (1991); Art. XIV, Sec. 5(5)

title: The pork barrel line of cases
ask: Trace the four cases on the pork barrel in order, with each holding.
items: Philconsa v. Enriquez (1994): CDF upheld; legislators merely recommend
LAMP (2012): PDAF upheld for want of proof; presumptions of constitutionality and regularity
Belgica (2013): PDAF void; Philconsa and LAMP abandoned on this point
Belgica (2019): lump sums not per se pork; valid if one singular purpose
src: Philconsa v. Enriquez; LAMP; Belgica (2013); Belgica (2019)

title: Elements of the congressional pork barrel
ask: How did Belgica (2013) define the congressional pork barrel (its elements)?
items: A lump-sum, discretionary fund
Legislators, individually or collectively as committees,
effectively control certain aspects of the fund’s utilization
through post-enactment measures or practices (identification, release, realignment)
src: Belgica v. Executive Secretary (2013)
hook: Presidential pork, by contrast: a lump-sum fund whose use the President decides.

title: Why the PDAF is unconstitutional (Belgica 2013)
ask: Which five constitutional principles did the PDAF violate in Belgica (2013)?
items: Separation of powers: legislators took part in budget execution after enactment
Non-delegability of legislative power: individual legislators effectively appropriated funds
Checks and balances: lump sum completed after enactment (‘budget within a budget’) leaves no proper item to veto
Accountability: legislators who take part in execution cannot oversee it; Congress cannot check its own members
Local autonomy: district representatives (national officers) substitute their judgment for local governments’ development plans
src: Belgica v. Executive Secretary (2013)
hook: ‘SNCAL’: Separation, Non-delegation, Checks, Accountability, Local autonomy.

title: Post-enactment acts barred to legislators
ask: After Belgica (2013), which post-enactment acts may legislators no longer perform, and what is left to Congress?
items: Identify projects after the budget is enacted
Take part in the release of funds
Realign their allocations (only the Sec. 25(5) officials may augment; Philconsa already said members only recommend)
Left to Congress after enactment: oversight only, by scrutiny and investigation
Identification was not merely recommendatory: the fund could not be used without it
src: Belgica (2013); Philconsa v. Enriquez; ABAKADA

title: Why the PDAF challenge failed in LAMP
ask: Why was the LAMP (2012) petition against the PDAF dismissed?
items: Presumption of constitutionality of the appropriation law
Presumption of regularity in the release of PDAF funds
Media reports, conjecture and general allegations are speculation, not proof
No evidence that DBM released funds directly to legislators or that they controlled spending
Dictum: after enactment Congress’s role is oversight; budget execution belongs to the Executive
Belgica (2013) later held LAMP no bar: it decided nothing on the merits
src: LAMP v. Secretary of Budget and Management (2012)

title: Belgica on the President’s discretionary funds
ask: What did Belgica (2013) hold on the Malampaya Fund and the Presidential Social Fund?
items: Presidential discretionary funds are not per se unconstitutional
The decrees creating them are appropriations made by law
But their use must meet valid-delegation standards (completeness and sufficient standard)
Void: ‘and for such other purposes as may be hereafter directed by the President’ (Malampaya, PD 910)
Void: ‘to finance the priority infrastructure development projects’ (Presidential Social Fund, PD 1869 as amended)
src: Belgica v. Executive Secretary (2013)

title: Singular correspondence: valid and invalid items
ask: Under the rule of singular correspondence, when is an appropriation item valid and when is it invalid?
items: Valid line item: a specified singular amount for a specified singular purpose, vetoable as a unit
Valid lump sum: funds several programs, projects or activities all under one singular purpose (Belgica 2019)
That purpose may be as general or specific as Congress wishes, if it does not negate the item veto
Invalid: multiple unrelated purposes, or vague and amorphous purposes
Invalid: amounts and projects chosen after enactment, especially by legislators (PDAF)
An item for a Major Final Output covers its integral components, e.g., license plates (Dela Cruz)
src: Belgica (2013); Belgica (2019); Dela Cruz v. Ochoa (2018)

title: Belgica (2019): lump-sum funds upheld
ask: Name the four 2014 GAA lump-sum funds upheld in Belgica (2019) and why they passed.
items: Unprogrammed Fund
Contingent Fund
E-Government Fund
Local Government Support Fund
Why: each had one singular purpose
Why: each had sufficient standards to guide execution
Why: no post-enactment discretion by legislators, and the item veto was not negated
src: Belgica v. Executive Secretary (2019)
hook: ‘U-C-E-L’: Unprogrammed, Contingent, E-Gov, Local Gov Support.

title: Item veto and inappropriate provisions (Philconsa)
ask: State the item veto rules from Art. VI, Sec. 27(2) and Philconsa v. Enriquez.
items: Item veto applies only to appropriation, revenue and tariff bills; elsewhere the veto is all-or-nothing
Vetoing an item does not affect the items the President does not object to
An item is an indivisible sum for a stated purpose: vetoed whole or not at all
An inappropriate provision (rider) may be vetoed separately, as if it were an item
An appropriate provision or condition can be struck only by vetoing the item it qualifies
Vetoed items return to Congress, which may override by two-thirds of all the Members of each House
src: Art. VI, Sec. 27(1)–(2); Philconsa v. Enriquez (1994)

title: Marks of an ‘inappropriate provision’ (rider) in the GAA
ask: What makes a GAA provision an ‘inappropriate provision’ under Art. VI, Sec. 25(2) and Philconsa, and what are examples?
items: It does not relate specifically to a particular appropriation in the GAA
It amends substantive law
It belongs in separate legislation
Example: letting SUCs keep their income in revolving funds (amended existing law; veto upheld)
Example: a GAA provision letting DBM change agencies’ organizational structures
Example: the PhilHealth fund-sweep provision that repealed the UHC Act’s reserve-fund rule (Pimentel 2025)
Not a rider: a condition that relates to the agency’s appropriation, e.g., defunding a unit
src: Art. VI, Sec. 25(2); Philconsa v. Enriquez; Pimentel v. House (2025); rule map news notes

title: Philconsa: vetoes struck down and vetoes upheld
ask: In Philconsa v. Enriquez, which three vetoes were void, and which two notable vetoes were upheld?
items: Void: veto of the debt-service provision limiting the fund to principal and interest of foreign and domestic debt
Void: veto of the DPWH rule that road maintenance be 70% by contract and 30% by administration
Void: veto of the special provision on AFP purchases of medicines
Reason they were void: appropriate conditions inseparable from their items, vetoed without the items
Upheld: veto of letting SUCs keep their income in revolving funds (amended existing law)
Upheld: veto of letting the AFP Chief of Staff augment pension funds from savings (contrary to Sec. 25(5))
src: Philconsa v. Enriquez (1994)

title: Officials who may augment from savings
ask: Which five officials may, by law, be authorized to augment items under Art. VI, Sec. 25(5)?
items: The President
The President of the Senate
The Speaker of the House of Representatives
The Chief Justice of the Supreme Court
The heads of the Constitutional Commissions
src: Art. VI, Sec. 25(5); Philconsa v. Enriquez; Pimentel v. House (2025)
hook: Not on the list: the Vice President, department secretaries (Finance: Pimentel 2025), the AFP Chief of Staff (Philconsa), individual legislators.

title: Requisites of a valid augmentation
ask: What are the requisites of a valid transfer or augmentation under Art. VI, Sec. 25(5) (Araullo)?
items: A law (usually the GAA) authorizes the official to augment
The funds are actual savings generated from the official’s own office’s appropriations
The purpose is to augment an existing item in the GAA for the official’s own office
So no ‘cross-border’ transfers to another branch or constitutional body
src: Art. VI, Sec. 25(5); Araullo v. Aquino III (2014); Demetria v. Alba
hook: Araullo states three requisites; the rule map splits ‘own office’ into a fourth. Law, Savings, Existing item, Own office.

title: What counts as ‘savings’
ask: Under the GAA definition applied in Araullo, what are savings, and what is not?
items: Balances of programmed appropriations, free from obligation, still available after the purpose was completed, finally discontinued or abandoned
Balances from unfilled (vacant) positions or leaves of absence without pay
Balances from improved systems and efficiencies that deliver the required outputs at lower cost
Not savings: unobligated allotments withdrawn and declared ‘savings’ before the end of the fiscal year
There can be no savings until the item has been fully provided for and its purpose satisfied
src: Araullo v. Aquino III (2014), applying the GAA

title: DAP practices struck down (Araullo)
ask: Which DAP practices did Araullo (2014) declare unconstitutional, and what of the DAP survived?
items: Withdrawing unobligated allotments and declaring them ‘savings’ before year-end, contrary to the GAA’s definition
Cross-border transfers of Executive savings to offices outside the Executive (e.g., COA, the House)
Funding programs, activities and projects not covered by any GAA appropriation
Using unprogrammed funds without the National Treasurer’s certification that revenues exceeded targets
DAP as a fiscal strategy was not itself void
Operative fact: completed projects stand; authors and implementors presumed in good faith, liability for proper tribunals (2015)
src: Araullo v. Aquino III (2014; Res. 2015)

title: Invalid transfers of appropriations: case map
ask: Name the forms of invalid transfer or augmentation and the case for each.
items: Blanket authority to move any fund to any project (Demetria v. Alba)
Mid-year ‘savings’ from withdrawn allotments (Araullo)
Cross-border transfers to another branch or body (Araullo)
Augmenting a non-existent item, e.g., unfunded benefits (Nazareth; Araullo)
Unprogrammed funds without excess-revenue certification (Araullo)
Postponing an election to free its funds for other uses (Macalintal 2023)
Augmentation by an official not named in Sec. 25(5) (AFP Chief: Philconsa; Finance Secretary: Pimentel 2025)
Realignment by individual legislators (Philconsa; Belgica)
src: Art. VI, Sec. 25(5); Demetria; Araullo; Nazareth; Macalintal (2023); Philconsa; Belgica; Pimentel (2025)

title: Nazareth, Pichay and Dela Cruz: one-line rules
ask: State the appropriation rule of Nazareth, Pichay and Dela Cruz.
items: Nazareth: a benefits law does not itself authorize payment; there must be an appropriation (Sec. 29(1))
Nazareth: savings cannot augment a non-existent item; the presidential approval covered only 1998–2000, so 2001 was disallowed
Pichay: the President may reorganize his own office (Admin. Code, Sec. 31) and fund it by realigning OP savings under the GAA
Dela Cruz: an item for a Major Final Output includes its integral components; specificity met if purpose is discernible and vetoable
src: Nazareth v. Villar (2013); Pichay (2012); Dela Cruz v. Ochoa (2018)

title: Madera rules on return of disallowed amounts
ask: State the Madera (2020) rules on who must return disallowed amounts.
items: Notice of disallowance set aside: no one returns anything
Approving and certifying officers in good faith, regular performance of duties, with diligence: not civilly liable
Approving and certifying officers in bad faith, malice or gross negligence: solidarily liable for the net disallowed amount
Payees (officers or passive recipients) return what each received, even in good faith (solutio indebiti)
Unless the amount was genuinely given for services rendered
Or the Court excuses return for undue prejudice, social justice, or other bona fide exceptions, case by case
src: Madera v. COA (2020)
hook: Net disallowed amount = total disallowed less what payees are excused from returning.

title: Badges of good faith of approving officers (Madera)
ask: What are the five badges of good faith of approving and certifying officers under Madera?
items: Certificates of availability of funds
An in-house or DOJ legal opinion
No precedent disallowing a similar case
A long agency practice with no prior disallowance
A reasonable textual reading of the law supporting legality
src: Madera v. COA (2020)

title: Valid postponement of elections (Macalintal 2023)
ask: What are the Macalintal (2023) guidelines for a valid postponement of elections?
items: An important, substantial or compelling reason, e.g., a public emergency
Only if and to the extent strictly required by the exigencies
The reason must mainly be to safeguard suffrage or other fundamental rights, or meet a public emergency
Elections must still be held at regular intervals that are not unduly long
Elections must remain free, honest, orderly and safe, safeguarding the right of suffrage
Not enough alone: election fatigue, divisiveness, shortness of the existing term, or other superficial or farcical reasons
src: Macalintal v. COMELEC (2023)

title: Why RA 11935 (BSKE postponement) was void
ask: Why was RA 11935 postponing the December 2022 barangay and SK elections void, and what followed?
items: It served no legitimate government interest: its real aim was to realign COMELEC’s election funds
A disguised transfer of appropriations, barred by Sec. 25(5)
Only the COMELEC Chairperson may augment COMELEC items, from COMELEC savings (fiscal autonomy)
It arbitrarily burdened the right of suffrage
Operative fact: the October 2023 elections proceeded; incumbents held over
src: Macalintal v. COMELEC (2023); Art. VI, Sec. 25(5)

title: Pimentel v. House (2025): PhilHealth fund sweep
ask: What did Pimentel v. House of Representatives (2025) hold on the PhilHealth fund transfer?
items: Congress cannot amend substantive laws through the GAA
GAA special provision and DOF circular void: repealed the UHC Act’s reserve-fund rule and conflicted with the Sin Tax law
The Finance Secretary cannot augment GAA items; only the President (Sec. 25(5))
₱60 billion ordered returned through the 2026 GAA; further transfers barred
No grave abuse in the President’s certification of urgency of the 2024 GAA
Caguioa, J.: also an inappropriate provision (Sec. 25(2)) and a breach of the special-fund rule (Sec. 29(3))
src: Pimentel v. House of Representatives (Dec. 3, 2025) (news; not in the syllabus)

title: Confidential and intelligence funds: rules
ask: What constitutional rules govern confidential and intelligence funds (2016 midterm; OVP controversy)?
items: They must be appropriated by law for a specific office and purpose
Moving them to another office mid-year is a prohibited transfer of appropriations
Congress may delete or reduce them, but may not increase the President’s recommendation
They remain subject to COA audit
src: Art. VI, Secs. 25(1), 25(5), 29(1); rule map news note

title: The four rules of Art. VI, Sec. 28
ask: State the four paragraphs of Art. VI, Sec. 28.
items: (1) Taxation shall be uniform and equitable; Congress shall evolve a progressive system of taxation
(2) Congress may, by law, authorize the President to fix tariff rates, quotas, dues and imposts within limits
(3) Charitable institutions, churches, mosques, non-profit cemeteries and property actually, directly and exclusively used for religious, charitable or educational purposes are exempt
(4) No tax exemption law without the concurrence of a majority of all the Members of the Congress
src: Art. VI, Sec. 28(1)–(4)

title: Uniform, equitable, progressive
ask: What does each of the three Sec. 28(1) standards of taxation mean, and which is enforceable?
items: Uniform: persons and things of the same class taxed at the same rate; reasonable classification allowed
Equitable: the burden falls in proportion to the ability to pay
Progressive: rates rise as the tax base rises
The progressive-system clause is a directive (‘shall evolve’), not an enforceable right; regressive taxes not barred (Tolentino)
src: Art. VI, Sec. 28(1); Tolentino v. Sec. of Finance

title: Valid classification in taxation (Tan v. Del Rosario)
ask: What are the four requisites of a valid classification under the uniformity rule (Tan v. Del Rosario)?
items: Rests on substantial distinctions
Germane to the purpose of the law
Not limited to existing conditions only
Applies equally to all members of the same class
src: Tan v. Del Rosario (1994); Art. VI, Sec. 28(1)
hook: The class reviewer says ‘substantial standards’; the correct word is ‘distinctions’.

title: What Congress may let the President fix (Sec. 28(2))
ask: Which five levies may Congress authorize the President to fix under Art. VI, Sec. 28(2)?
items: Tariff rates
Import and export quotas
Tonnage dues
Wharfage dues
Other duties or imposts
src: Art. VI, Sec. 28(2); Garcia v. Executive Secretary

title: Conditions on the tariff delegation
ask: What four conditions does Art. VI, Sec. 28(2) attach to the President’s power to fix tariffs?
items: Authorized by Congress by law
Within specified limits
Subject to such limitations and restrictions as Congress may impose
Within the framework of the national development program of the Government
src: Art. VI, Sec. 28(2); Garcia v. Executive Secretary

title: Garcia v. Executive Secretary: holdings
ask: Why were the EOs imposing extra duties on crude oil valid in Garcia v. Executive Secretary?
items: Sec. 28(2) expressly allows Congress to delegate tariff-fixing to the President
Tariff and Customs Code Sec. 401 lets him act for the national economy, general welfare and/or national security
Protecting local industries is not the only permissible aim
A tariff measure is not void just because it mainly raises revenue
No origination problem: the President acted under a statute Congress enacted
src: Garcia v. Executive Secretary (1992)

title: Constitutionally tax-exempt (Sec. 28(3))
ask: List what Art. VI, Sec. 28(3) exempts from taxation.
items: Charitable institutions
Churches, and parsonages or convents appurtenant thereto
Mosques
Non-profit cemeteries
All lands, buildings and improvements actually, directly and exclusively used for religious, charitable or educational purposes
src: Art. VI, Sec. 28(3)

title: Requisites of the charitable exemption (Lung Center)
ask: What must a claimant prove to enjoy the Sec. 28(3) charitable exemption from real property tax (Lung Center)?
items: The institution is charitable
Its property is actually used for charitable purposes
directly used for charitable purposes
and exclusively (solely) used for charitable purposes
Burden of proof on the claimant; exemption strictly construed against it
src: Art. VI, Sec. 28(3); Lung Center v. Quezon City (2004)
hook: Two requisites, the second with three adverbs: actually, directly, exclusively.

title: Lung Center: rules on charitable character and use
ask: State the Lung Center rules on what makes an institution charitable and which property is exempt.
items: Test: does it exist for a purpose recognized in law as charitable, or for gain, profit or private advantage?
Charging paying patients does not defeat charitable character
Receiving government subsidies does not defeat it either
It is the use of the property, not the use of its income, that counts
Portions leased for commercial use (clinics, canteen, stores, garden center) are taxable
Portions used for patients, paying or non-paying, are exempt
src: Lung Center of the Philippines v. Quezon City (2004)

title: Who may grant tax exemptions (John Hay)
ask: Under John Hay PAC v. Lim, who may grant tax exemptions?
items: Congress, by law concurred in by a majority of all its Members (Sec. 28(4))
The Constitution itself (e.g., Art. VI, Sec. 28(3); Art. XIV, Sec. 4(3)–(4))
Local governments, but only from local taxes
Never the President by proclamation
src: John Hay PAC v. Lim (2003); Art. VI, Sec. 28(4)

title: Rules on statutory tax exemptions
ask: What rules govern a statutory tax exemption?
items: Only by law passed with the concurrence of a majority of all the Members of the Congress
Must be expressly granted, in language too clear to be mistaken; never implied
Strictly construed against the claimant
Claimant bears the burden of proving the exemption
An exemption granted to one zone does not extend to others unless the law says so (Subic, not John Hay)
src: Art. VI, Sec. 28(4); John Hay PAC v. Lim; Lung Center

title: John Hay PAC v. Lim: holdings
ask: What did John Hay PAC v. Lim hold on Proclamation 420?
items: RA 7227’s tax incentives were intended for the Subic zone only; no express extension to later zones
Sec. 3 of Proc. 420 (Subic incentives for John Hay) void: circumvents the majority-of-all-Members rule
The other privileges are matters Congress traditionally legislates: unwarranted delegation
The creation of the John Hay Special Economic Zone itself stood
src: John Hay PAC v. Lim (2003)

title: Origination rules (Tolentino v. Sec. of Finance)
ask: State the rules on origination of revenue bills from Tolentino v. Secretary of Finance.
items: The bill, not the law, must originate in the House
The Senate may propose amendments, even a substitute bill; the law need not be substantially the House bill
The Senate may file its substitute in anticipation, if it withholds action as a body until the House bill arrives
Why the House: district representatives are closer to local needs; senators, elected at large, bring the national view
Insisting on the House version would deny the Senate’s power to amend, break co-equality, and make the House superior
src: Art. VI, Sec. 24; Tolentino v. Secretary of Finance (1994)

title: Tolentino v. Sec. of Finance: other holdings
ask: Apart from origination, what else did Tolentino v. Secretary of Finance hold on the E-VAT law?
items: A bicameral conference committee may insert entirely new provisions found in neither version, if germane
A presidential certification of urgency dispenses with printing three days before passage
It also dispenses with readings on three separate days
Uniformity: the VAT applies equally to all similarly situated
Progressive taxation is a directive, not an enforceable right
The VAT, a general tax, does not single out the press or religion
src: Tolentino v. Secretary of Finance (1994); Art. VI, Sec. 26(2)

title: What the President can do with a revenue bill he opposes
ask: A House-initiated income tax reform bill passes over the President’s objections (2015 midterm). What are the steps and options?
items: Origination is satisfied if the bill came from the House
The President’s objections matter only once the bill reaches him
He may veto the whole bill
Or veto particular items, since it is a revenue bill (Sec. 27(2))
If he does not act within 30 days of receipt, it becomes law
Congress may override by two-thirds of all the Members of each House
src: Art. VI, Secs. 24, 27(1)–(2); rule map 2015 midterm note

title: Votes and numbers on money and tax measures
ask: Give the vote thresholds and time periods that govern money and tax measures.
items: Tax exemption law: concurrence of a majority of all the Members of the Congress (Sec. 28(4))
Veto override, including vetoed items: two-thirds of all the Members of each House (Sec. 27(1))
President acts on a bill within 30 days of receipt, or it becomes law (Sec. 27(1))
Budget submitted within 30 days from the opening of every regular session (Art. VII, Sec. 22)
Certified urgent bills: no three-day printing and no readings on separate days (Sec. 26(2); Tolentino)
src: Art. VI, Secs. 26(2), 27(1), 28(4); Art. VII, Sec. 22

title: Purposes of taxation
ask: What are the three purposes of the power of taxation (class reviewer)?
items: To raise revenue
As a tool for regulation
Protection (the ‘power to keep alive’)
src: Class reviewer (inherent powers: taxation)
